### Recommendation

I strongly recommend using C++ `std::sort` for this task. The standard library implementation, typically based on Introsort, is highly optimized and carefully engineered by experts to handle diverse data distributions robustly. For ten million doubles, `std::sort` will consistently outperform a naive, custom QuickSort due to sophisticated optimizations like三路 partitioning, small-subarray insertion switches, and fallaxes to Heapsort to guarantee $O(N \log N)$ worst-case performance. Writing a custom sort introduces significant maintenance overhead and likely lower performance unless you invest months in tuning cache locality and branch prediction, which rarely pays off for general use cases. Relying on `std::sort` ensures you leverage decades of compiler and library refinements, minimizing bugs and maximizing execution speed for uniform random data.

### Supporting basis

The primary consideration is algorithmic robustness and constant-factor efficiency. `std::sort` avoids the catastrophic $O(N^2)$ behavior of naive QuickSort on specific inputs, ensuring predictable performance. While uniform random data is generally favorable for QuickSort, Introsort’s hybrid approach still extracts better cache performance and reduces recursive overhead compared to manual implementations. Furthermore, modern compilers can aggressively optimize standard library calls using specialization and inline hints, whereas custom code may miss these opportunities. The time spent debugging and profiling a custom QuickSort to match `std::sort`’s speed is better invested in other parts of your program. Given the data size and distribution, the marginal gain from a custom implementation is negligible, while the risk of subtle bugs or performance regressions on different hardware platforms is high. Therefore, standard library usage is the superior practical choice.<|im_end|>
